s0w: Trauma-Informed Care: Becoming a Safe Place
s1w: Being trauma-informed does not mean being an expert. It means being willing to learn, notice and respond with care. Trauma is not only what happened; it is how what happened overwhelmed a person's ability to cope, so that the body and heart can still live as if it is happening now. A trauma-informed person, family or church makes safety come first, so healing can begin.

s35w: Jesus is the model. He was sent "to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives" (Isaiah 61:1). He made people safe before He guided them: He refused to condemn the woman brought to Him, stayed calm with the tormented man among the tombs, and began His great sermon with blessings for the grieving and crushed. He entered suffering Himself, so He is a High Priest "touched with the feeling of our infirmities" (Hebrews 4:15).
s36w: You do not have to be an expert to help hurting people. Be safe, calm and kind, ask before you act, and help them find more support.
s37w: Trauma and the Whole Person: Spirit, Soul and Body
s38w: We are made of spirit, soul and body (1 Thessalonians 5:23), and trauma can touch all three. The body keeps the alarm ringing; the soul (mind, will and emotions) can be put "on hold" while we are in survival mode; and the spirit can feel cut off, unworthy or abandoned by God. Healing cares for all three together.
s39w: alarm reactions to reminders (fight, flight, freeze, fawn)
s53w: Soul goes "on hold" (cannot think or feel clearly)
s57w: Where do I feel this in my body?
s59w: What has this done to how I see God?
s61w: room to feel and make sense
s62w: restored identity and belonging with God
s63w: Spiritual problems need only spiritual answers
s64w: If I still hurt, I have not healed
s65w: Settle the body first: breath, feet on the floor, a safe place
s66w: Make room for the soul: name and feel the emotions, lament
s67w: Restore the spirit: truth about God's love, safe community, prayer at a gentle pace
s68w: "I pray God your whole spirit and soul and body be preserved blameless" (1 Thessalonians 5:23). God cares for the whole person. Jesus healed bodies, restored dignity and forgave sins. The Holy Spirit is called the Comforter, the One who tends to our hearts, not only to our beliefs.
s69w: Hard things can hurt our body, our thoughts and feelings, and our closeness to God. God heals all of us.
s70w: Strongholds: When Thought Patterns Become Walls
s71w: Trauma can make thinking rigid. A thought repeated becomes an automatic thought; automatic thoughts become patterns; patterns become mindsets; and mindsets become strongholds: walls in the mind built to protect us, like the walls of Jericho. Because the brain can be renewed, these walls can come down through God's Spirit, honest processing, safe relationships and practising new thoughts.
s72w: tension when the old belief is challenged
s78w: I am too much and not enough
s80w: avoiding situations that might prove them wrong
s81w: the same reactions in new places
s85w: Becomes a pattern, then a mindset
s86w: Stronghold: a wall that keeps out danger and also keeps out love
s87w: Which of my "walls" were built to protect me?
s88w: What lie does this wall defend?
s89w: What truth does God speak instead?
s94w: If I still think it, I have failed
s95w: Name the thought and the wall it builds
s96w: Trace where it began, with compassion
s97w: Bring it to God and a safe person
s98w: Speak and practise the truth daily
s99w: Expect gradual change, like a path in grass
s100w: "The weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds" (2 Corinthians 10:4). God brought down Jericho's walls, and He renews our minds (Romans 12:2). He does not shame us for building walls to survive; He gently replaces them with Himself as our true fortress (Psalm 18:2).
s101w: Old hurtful thoughts can become like walls in our mind. With God's truth, practice and safe people, the walls can come down.
s102w: Vicarious Trauma: When Helpers Absorb Pain
s103w: People who care for the hurting (pastors, counsellors, leaders, nurses, parents and friends) can slowly absorb the trauma they hear. This is vicarious or secondary trauma. It can look like exhaustion, numbness, cynicism, intrusive images or losing joy in ministry. Healthy helpers heal and rest, so they can keep helping.

s108w: If I rest, people will suffer
s109w: I should be able to carry this

s122w: Who do I talk to about what I carry?

s136w: Even Jesus withdrew to quiet places to pray (Luke 5:16) and told His tired disciples, "Come ye yourselves apart... and rest a while" (Mark 6:31). Moses was taught to share the load (Exodus 18:18). Healed people heal people, and God cares for the carers.
s137w: People who help others can get very tired inside. Helpers need rest, support and care too.
s138w: C.A.R.E. 1 – Consent: Ask Before You Act
s140w: Restore dignity by asking permission before you pray, touch or advise.
s141w: Pause before you act on your care
s142w: Ask: "Would you like me to pray with you?" or "Would a hug help, or would you rather not?"
s143w: Ask before giving advice: "Would it help if I shared a thought?"
s144w: Give a clear time frame: "I can stay with you for the next ten minutes"
s145w: Accept a "no" warmly, with no pressure or guilt
s147w: Asking shows respect; most people feel honoured
s149w: Say "That's okay" and stay present; you can pray quietly later
s151w: Ask first; advice without permission often feels like pressure
s152w: Trauma often involves having choices taken away. Asking permission gives back a sense of control, which calms the threat system and builds trust.
s153w: Before you pray for someone, hug them or give advice, ask them first. Their "no" is okay.
s154w: C.A.R.E. 2 – Attune: Hear the Story Beneath the Story
s156w: Tune in like a radio dial: be present, notice and reflect.
s157w: Turn towards the person and slow down
s158w: Listen to tone, body language and feelings, not just words
s159w: Reflect back: "It sounds like this has been really heavy for you"
s160w: Validate: "That makes sense. I'm here with you"
s161w: Resist the urge to correct, compare or quote verses too soon
s162w: I don't know what to say
s165w: Let them; offer tissues and quiet
s167w: Bring the focus gently back to them
s168w: Feeling understood activates the social engagement system, settling heart rate and breathing. Reflecting feelings helps the other person's brain put experience into words.
s169w: Listen carefully, notice how they feel, and say back what you heard. Being with them is more important than having answers.
s172w: Calm your own body first, then help theirs settle.
s173w: Notice your own breathing and slow it; relax your shoulders
s175w: Invite grounding: "Can we take a slow breath together and feel our feet on the floor?"
s176w: Help them notice one comforting thing in the room
s177w: Name and normalise: "Your body is reacting to stress. That is normal after what you have been through"
s178w: They are too upset to breathe slowly
s179w: Just breathe slowly yourself; nervous systems borrow calm
s181w: Use gentle, simple choices and warm tone
s184w: Nervous systems co-regulate: a calm, regulated person helps another person's body settle, so the thinking brain can come back online.
s185w: First calm your own body. Then help them breathe slowly and feel their feet on the floor. Tell them their reaction is normal.
s186w: C.A.R.E. 4 – Empower: Choice, Strength and Next Steps
s188w: Give back voice, choice and hope.
s189w: Offer simple choices: "Would you like to sit here or step outside?"
s190w: Ask what has helped them before
s191w: Point out a strength: "It took courage to share this"
s192w: Share one skill they can use (a breath, grounding, a lament)
s193w: Offer further help: a counsellor, doctor, support group or helpline
s195w: Offer two options and let them choose
s197w: Empowering means walking with, not carrying for
s198w: They need more than I can give
s199w: Referring on is love, not failure
s200w: A sense of agency reduces helplessness, which is at the core of trauma. Naming strengths strengthens self-efficacy, and connecting people with support widens their safety net.
s201w: Let the person make choices, remind them of their strengths, and help them find more support.
s204w: Take apart one old mental wall, brick by brick.
s205w: Write down a thought that keeps coming back (for example, "No one can be trusted")
s206w: Trace it: when did this wall first help you survive? Thank God it protected you then
s207w: Name the cost: what love, joy or freedom does it keep out now?
s208w: Find God's truth that answers it, and write it in your own words
s209w: Practise the new thought daily for 30 days, and share it with a safe person
s211w: Feelings lag behind truth; keep practising
s212w: I feel ashamed of the wall
s213w: Walls were built to survive; there is no condemnation
s215w: Each repetition of truth wears a new path
s216w: Repeating new, believable thoughts while feeling safe strengthens new neural pathways, and old patterns weaken with disuse. This is neuroplasticity at work.
s217w: Some old thoughts are like walls in your mind. Find the true words God says and repeat them every day until the wall comes down.
s220w: Put down what you carried today, so compassion can last.
s221w: After a heavy conversation, take three slow breaths and notice your feet
s222w: Write or say what you heard that is still with you
s223w: Hand it to God in a short prayer: "This is Yours to carry"
s224w: Do something that tells your body the day is done (walk, wash your hands, change clothes)
s225w: Once a week, debrief with a trusted person or supervisor
s227w: Releasing it to God is not abandoning them
s228w: I have no one to debrief with
s229w: Ask a mentor, counsellor or fellow leader
s230w: It keeps coming back at night
s231w: Write it down and pray before sleep; seek support if it continues
s232w: Short rituals that mark the end of care help the nervous system switch from alert to rest, and regular debriefing protects helpers from secondary traumatic stress.
s233w: After you help someone with a heavy story, breathe, pray and give the burden to God. Then do something that helps your body rest.
